The seasons must follow their proper order. The discourse on timely snow states: “The key to harmonizing and regulating the four seasons lies with the ruler of living beings. Whether rich and honored or poor and lowly, one should have a way of maintaining vigilance and reflection [?].” Is this not a mind devoted to careful self-cultivation without slackening? Even a moment deserves to be cherished. The record of spring’s light states: “This spring has already passed, yet my studies remain incomplete. Though another spring will come, it will not be the fresh spring of this year.” Is this not a mind that strives unceasingly to improve itself? It says: “The mind is empty within, not solid, so that spiritual intelligence may dwell there.” It says: “Among people in this world, it is often the spirit that directs the mind, rather than the mind that directs the spirit.” These are expressions in the composition ‘Questioning the Mind’ [?]. It says: …

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
今人之心法古賢善者少效古愚惡者多
曰古人以卑而致高以愚而致賢捨此而
取彼守虧而樂安省頑之文也善惡之幾
決擇之術蓋有以正乎人心矣曰全順其
宜而爲之則身乎蕩蕩曰若完其肌膚而
全其體則運用陰陽此常道不過則無虧
矣保身說也曰勤者當色而不色爲慮有
三惰者奉且薄却乃顏色美爲忘志而不
慮曰慱學匪行不若無簡藝精專以爲用
勤惰之說也存養之嚴取舍之辨眞足以
警乎人心矣
===
宸章炫燿播在臣工勑天之歌厥旨無二是奚
假于丹扆六箴之陳千秋金鑑錄之進也
哉愚也以是知
太祖之道體仁之道也
太祖之學盡心之學也
太祖之文虞舜之文也
列聖相承是彝是訓肆我
punctuated:
「今人之心，法古賢善者少，效古愚惡者多。」曰：「古人以卑而致高，以愚而致賢。捨此而取彼，守虧而樂安。」《省頑》之文也。善惡之幾，決擇之術，蓋有以正乎人心矣。曰：「全順其宜而爲之，則身乎蕩蕩。」曰：「若完其肌膚而全其體，則運用陰陽，此常道不過，則無虧矣。」《保身說》也。曰：「勤者當色而不色，爲慮有三；惰者奉且薄，却乃顏色美，爲忘志而不慮。」曰：「慱學匪行，不若無；簡藝精專，以爲用。」《勤惰》之說也。存養之嚴，取舍之辨，眞足以警乎人心矣。
宸章炫燿，播在臣工，勑天之歌，厥旨無二。是奚假于《丹扆六箴》之陳、《千秋金鑑錄》之進也哉！愚也以是知太祖之道，體仁之道也；太祖之學，盡心之學也；太祖之文，虞舜之文也。列聖相承，是彝是訓，肆我
translation_en:
…“Among people today, few take the worthy and good of antiquity as models for their hearts; many imitate the foolish and wicked of antiquity.” It says: “The ancients rose from lowliness to eminence and from foolishness to worthiness. Yet people abandon this and choose that, persist in their deficiencies, and delight in ease.” These are words from Awakening the Stubborn (Xing wan). In discerning the first stirrings of good and evil and explaining how to choose between them, they surely serve to rectify people’s hearts. It says: “Act wholly in accordance with what is fitting, and one’s person will be expansive and untroubled [?].” It also says: “If you would preserve your flesh and keep your body whole, then work with yin and yang; if you do not transgress this constant Way, there will be no impairment.” This is the Explanation of Preserving the Person (Bao shen shuo). It says: “The diligent, though they ought to show it in their countenance, do not [?], for they have three concerns; the idle, though their sustenance is meager, nevertheless look well, because they forget their aspirations and give no thought to them [?].” It says: “Broad learning without practice is worse than none; select an art and master it through concentrated effort, so that it may be put to use [?].” This is the discussion of diligence and idleness. Its rigor in preserving and nurturing the heart, and its discrimination between what to accept and what to reject, are truly sufficient to admonish people’s hearts.
The imperial writings shine brilliantly and circulate among the officials. Their purport is wholly at one with the song enjoining attentiveness to Heaven. What need, then, is there to present the Six Admonitions for the Vermilion Screen (Dan yi liu zhen), or to submit the Record of the Golden Mirror for a Thousand Autumns (Qianqiu jin jian lu)? From this I, in my ignorance, understand that Taizu’s Way is the Way of embodying benevolence; Taizu’s learning is the learning of fully realizing the heart; and Taizu’s writings are writings like those of Yu Shun. The succession of sage emperors has inherited these constant principles and these teachings. Thus our…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
皇上聰明睿智文武聖神仁溢海隅心契冲漠
是故情深而文明誠中而形外其著之訓
典彰之話言者尤爲不可殫述焉然大虛
之量管窺難窺滄海之涯蠡亦思測固嘗
服習之而若有所知矣何者
大享之禮崇報本之
典也禮成一
詔恩覃臣民推尊
親之心以及天下之親澤普而不私惠流而靡
竭矣承天之狩展謁
===
陵之
孝也蠲租一
詔德沛多方推孝
親之心以及所經之地道光而不匱恩洽而無
餘矣其
詔令抑何仁也至若仲夏寫懷之什重小人之
依思田功之艱憫農之心溢于言表其仁
之隨感而應者乎是
punctuated:
皇上聰明睿智，文武聖神，仁溢海隅，心契冲漠。是故情深而文明，誠中而形外。其著之訓典、彰之話言者，尤爲不可殫述焉。然大虛之量，管窺難窺；滄海之涯，蠡亦思測。固嘗服習之，而若有所知矣。何者？
大享之禮，崇報本之典也。禮成一詔，恩覃臣民，推尊親之心以及天下之親，澤普而不私，惠流而靡竭矣。承天之狩，展謁陵之孝也。蠲租一詔，德沛多方，推孝親之心以及所經之地，道光而不匱，恩洽而無餘矣。其詔令抑何仁也！至若《仲夏寫懷》之什，重小人之依，思田功之艱，憫農之心溢于言表，其仁之隨感而應者乎？是
translation_en:
…His Majesty is perceptive and wise, accomplished in civil and military affairs, sagely and divinely discerning. His benevolence extends to the farthest shores, and his mind accords with the profound stillness of the formless. Thus his deep feelings find expression in brilliant writing, and his inner sincerity manifests itself outwardly. What he has set down in authoritative instructions and made manifest in instructive pronouncements is especially impossible to recount in full. Yet the immensity of the great void is hard to glimpse through a narrow tube, and one still hopes to measure the bounds of the vast sea with a gourd scoop. I have indeed repeatedly studied these writings and seem to have gained some understanding. How so?
The rite of the Great Sacrifice honors the ceremony of repaying one’s origins. When the rite was completed, a single edict extended grace to officials and common people alike. His Majesty extended his devotion to honoring his parent to encompass the parents of all under Heaven: his beneficence was universal and impartial, and his bounty flowed without exhaustion. His imperial tour to Chengtian expressed filial devotion through his visit to pay respects at the imperial mausoleum. A single edict remitting land taxes showered beneficence upon many regions. He extended his filial devotion to his parent to encompass the lands through which he passed: his Way shone without diminution, and his grace reached everywhere, leaving none outside it. How benevolent his edicts are! As for his poem Expressing My Feelings in Midsummer, it gives weight to what sustains the common people and reflects upon the hardships of agricultural labor. His compassion for farmers overflows beyond the words themselves. Is this not his benevolence responding to whatever moves him? This…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
皇上之仁即
太祖之仁也虞舜咨四岳之心又繼
太祖而紹之矣以至敬一之訓所以事心而立
極也則衍而爲箴以彰身教如曰肅于朝
廷愼于閒居曰行顧其言終如其始罔非
允迪之思布之學宮
聖學之本昭矣程氏四箴所以克復而求仁也
則翼之以註以廣其旨如曰弗使外物蕩
其中常使中制於外曰必求合諸道理凖
===
諸經傳罔非研幾之訓風之天下
聖學之精著矣是
製作一本于心也至若欽
天記頌之作切時保之心嚴昭事之道對越之
誠儼然如在其心學之大者乎是
皇上之心即
太祖之心也虞舜勑天之學又繼
太祖而紹之矣嗚呼匪開厥先無以繼不傳之
統匪紹厥後無以永開後之心是仁也心
punctuated: 皇上之仁，即太祖之仁也。虞舜咨四岳之心，又繼太祖而紹之矣。以至敬一之訓，所以事心而立極也，則衍而爲箴，以彰身教。如曰：「肅于朝廷，愼于閒居。」曰：「行顧其言，終如其始。」罔非允迪之思。布之學宮，聖學之本昭矣。程氏四箴，所以克復而求仁也，則翼之以註，以廣其旨。如曰：「弗使外物蕩其中，常使中制於外。」曰：「必求合諸道理，凖諸經傳。」罔非研幾之訓。風之天下，聖學之精著矣。是製作一本于心也。至若《欽天記頌》之作，切時保之心，嚴昭事之道，對越之誠，儼然如在，其心學之大者乎！是皇上之心，即太祖之心也。虞舜勑天之學，又繼太祖而紹之矣。嗚呼！匪開厥先，無以繼不傳之統；匪紹厥後，無以永開後之心。是仁也，心
translation_en: …His Majesty’s benevolence is precisely Taizu’s benevolence. The disposition with which Shun of Yu consulted the Four Mountains has once again been carried forward in succession to Taizu. As for the instruction on reverent single-mindedness, by which one cultivates the mind and establishes the supreme standard, His Majesty expanded it into admonitions to make manifest his teaching through personal example. These include: “Be reverent at court and cautious in private”; and “Let your conduct accord with your words, and finish as you began.” All express his concern for faithfully putting the Way into practice. Distributed to the schools, they illuminate the foundation of sagely learning. Master Cheng’s Four Admonitions provide the means to overcome the self, return to ritual propriety, and seek benevolence. His Majesty supplemented them with annotations to amplify their meaning. These include: “Do not allow external things to unsettle what is within; always let what is within govern what is without”; and “Always seek accord with moral principle and take the classics and their commentaries as your standard.” All teach the investigation of the subtlest beginnings. Disseminated to influence all under Heaven, they reveal the essential refinement of sagely learning. Thus these compositions are rooted wholly in the mind. As for the composition of the Record and Eulogy of Revering Heaven, it expresses an earnest resolve constantly to preserve Heaven’s favor [?] and a solemn commitment to serving Heaven illustriously. Its sincerity in standing before Heaven is reverent, as though Heaven were present: is this not the greatness of his learning of the mind? Thus His Majesty’s mind is precisely Taizu’s mind. Shun of Yu’s learning in reverently attending to Heaven has once again been carried forward in succession to Taizu. Alas! Without first opening the way, there would be no means to resume the interrupted succession; without carrying it forward afterward, there would be no means to perpetuate the intention of opening the way for posterity. This benevolence, this mind…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
也一本也道統之所在也我
太祖克紹于創業之初我
皇上大闡于中興之日續千載之眞傳衍將來
之心法信乎
聖人繼作非蕩蕩巍巍者不足以擬之也夫惟
如是故沛之
詔令則爲仁言發之
製作莫非心學觀于
聖人之文而全體大用可窺矣愚也生學未通經
===
聖誠不自知其淺且安也惟進而教之幸甚
言敢述
第二問
張旂
同考試官教諭廖　批〔六經聖人所以詔世者本明且備自厄于秦火雜于漢儒而窮經者迄無定論子能究極源委而折衷于宋儒之見是深于經者矣高薦允宜〕
考試官教諭盧　批〔斷以理是博而精者佳士佳士不冗不浮參酌諸儒異同歸一〕
punctuated:
也，一本也，道統之所在也。我太祖克紹于創業之初，我皇上大闡于中興之日，續千載之眞傳，衍將來之心法。信乎，聖人繼作，非蕩蕩巍巍者不足以擬之也。夫惟如是，故沛之詔令則爲仁言，發之製作莫非心學。觀于聖人之文，而全體大用可窺矣。愚也，生學未通經聖，誠不自知其淺且安也。惟進而教之，幸甚！言敢述。

第二問

張旂

同考試官教諭廖　批〔六經，聖人所以詔世者，本明且備。自厄于秦火，雜于漢儒，而窮經者迄無定論。子能究極源委，而折衷于宋儒之見，是深于經者矣。高薦允宜。〕

考試官教諭盧　批〔斷以理，是博而精者。佳士！佳士！不冗不浮，參酌諸儒異同歸一。〕
translation_en:
…is the heart; it is the single foundation, wherein lies the succession of the Way. Our Taizu successfully carried on this succession at the founding of the dynasty, and our Emperor has greatly elucidated it in this time of restoration, continuing the authentic transmission of a thousand years and extending the teaching of the heart into the future. Truly, as sages arise in succession, nothing short of vastness and sublimity suffices to describe them. Thus, when this finds abundant expression in imperial edicts, it becomes benevolent speech; when expressed in imperial compositions, it is invariably the learning of the heart. By examining the sage’s writings, one may glimpse its entire substance and full functioning. In my ignorance, my learning has not penetrated the Classics and the sages [?]; indeed, I am unaware of my own shallowness and complacency [?]. If you would bring me forward and instruct me, I should be most fortunate! I venture to set forth these words.

Second Question

Zhang Qi

Comment by Associate Examiner Liao, Instructor: 〔The Six Classics, through which the sages instructed the world, were originally clear and complete. Since suffering the calamity of the Qin book burning and becoming intermingled with the interpretations of Han scholars, however, those who investigate the Classics have reached no settled conclusions. You have thoroughly examined their origins and subsequent development, weighing the issues against the views of Song scholars. You are indeed deeply versed in the Classics. A recommendation for high placement is fully deserved.〕

Comment by Examiner Lu, Instructor: 〔You judge by principle: your learning is both broad and precise. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar! Neither verbose nor superficial, you weigh the similarities and differences among the various scholars and bring them into unity.〕

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
考試官學正丘　批〔明經之言〕
善稽古者探始慱遠而闕其疑善明經者
置謬存眞而弗戾乎古夫煩訓散經白首
而眩于從遂稽古難矣識其大而闕其疑
釋經不泥可也腐舌翳目管窺而易乎古
昔明經難矣從其善而識其餘互爲參考
可也何也道可以知窮事必以實著事之
既往跬步難尋况生于千載之下而臆決
于千載之上乎哉是知經以漢儒而雜亦
===
以漢儒而傳理明于宋儒而亦不可盡廢
乎訓詁也即是可以復明問矣嗚呼六經
孰明之孔子明之也抑孰晦之多言晦之
也蓋多言則義微多異則眞隱眩于前者
中人皆趨之而藏于幽者上知或昧聖人
者覈乎華實之辨安其先後之倫終審而
動參驗而言夫然後情以綜物而文以綱
世矣百家之紛若不循依太山之尊而誤
遊丘垤者乎後儒之臆決不循病子孫之
punctuated:
考試官學正丘，批〔明經之言〕

善稽古者，探始慱遠而闕其疑；善明經者，置謬存眞而弗戾乎古。夫煩訓散經，白首而眩于從，遂稽古難矣。識其大而闕其疑，釋經不泥可也。腐舌翳目，管窺而易乎古昔，明經難矣。從其善而識其餘，互爲參考可也。何也？道可以知窮，事必以實著。事之既往，跬步難尋，况生于千載之下，而臆決于千載之上乎哉？是知經以漢儒而雜，亦以漢儒而傳；理明于宋儒，而亦不可盡廢乎訓詁也。即是可以復明問矣。

嗚呼！六經孰明之？孔子明之也。抑孰晦之？多言晦之也。蓋多言則義微，多異則眞隱。眩于前者，中人皆趨之；而藏于幽者，上知或昧。聖人者，覈乎華實之辨，安其先後之倫，終審而動，參驗而言。夫然後情以綜物，而文以綱世矣。百家之紛，若不循依太山之尊而誤遊丘垤者乎？後儒之臆決，不循病子孫之
translation_en:
Examiner Qiu, School Instructor, comments: 〔Words that illuminate the Classics.〕

Those skilled in investigating antiquity trace beginnings, range widely into the distant past [?], and leave doubtful matters unresolved. Those skilled in elucidating the Classics set aside errors, preserve what is true, and do not depart from antiquity. When explanations proliferate and the Classics become fragmented, one may reach old age still bewildered about which interpretation to follow: investigating antiquity thus becomes difficult. It is acceptable to grasp the main import, leave doubtful matters unresolved, and interpret the Classics without becoming mired in particulars. When tongues wear out and eyes grow dim, yet one views things through a narrow tube and readily alters the understanding of antiquity, elucidating the Classics becomes difficult. It is acceptable to follow what is sound, take note of the rest, and use the various interpretations to check one another. Why is this? The Way can be fathomed through understanding, but events must be established through evidence. Once events have passed, even their smallest traces are hard to recover. How much less can someone born a thousand years later decide by conjecture what happened a thousand years before! We therefore know that although the Han scholars introduced heterogeneous elements into the Classics, they also transmitted them. Although the Song scholars clarified principle, textual exegesis cannot be discarded altogether. On this basis, I can answer your discerning question.

Alas! Who elucidated the Six Classics? Confucius elucidated them. And who obscured them? Excessive discourse obscured them. For when words multiply, meaning grows faint; when divergent interpretations multiply, truth becomes hidden. Ordinary people all hasten toward what dazzles before their eyes, while even the wisest may fail to perceive what lies concealed in obscurity. The sage scrutinizes the distinction between ornament and substance, sets their order of precedence aright, acts only after thorough examination, and speaks only after comparison and verification. Only then can his understanding of the true circumstances comprehend all things, and his writings provide an ordering framework for the world. Is the confusion of the hundred schools not like failing to seek the lofty eminence of Mount Tai and mistakenly wandering among little mounds [?]? As for the conjectural judgments of later scholars, are they not like lamenting that one’s descendants … [?]

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
弗類而索其似于途之夫也乎請卒言之
易肇于伏羲連山歸藏夏商之易不可見
矣文王係卦辭孔子作十翼之辭而易定
焉其後以卜筮得不火于秦漢興而易分
爲三焦贛易林外道而衍數竊其一偏昧
厥全體既非聖人之作田何傳之子夏得
卦象爻彖文言說卦十二篇之眞雖易之
本經而今則莫可考矣衍其說而傳之今
者非費直邪其徒陳元鄭康成等揚其波
===
而其學遂盛及王弼爲注高談理致而學
者益宗之然以彖象文言參解易爻使彖
象文言雜入卦中者直始之也故先儒謂
古經始變于費氏而目弼爲老易者非以
其抗高論而衍玄談乎然經雖變于費氏
而未遺乎經弼論雖過玄而經不隨之晦
也迨宋程子作傳亦惟觀其理而略于卦
畫之分屬于是朱子本義始集其成而行
于世矣書出于史官羲皇之上三墳不可
punctuated:
弗類，而索其似于途之夫也乎？請卒言之。易肇于伏羲，連山、歸藏，夏商之易，不可見矣。文王係卦辭，孔子作十翼之辭，而易定焉。其後以卜筮，得不火于秦。漢興，而易分爲三。焦贛易林，外道而衍數，竊其一偏，昧厥全體，既非聖人之作。田何傳之子夏，得卦象、爻彖、文言、說卦十二篇之眞，雖易之本經，而今則莫可考矣。衍其說而傳之今者，非費直邪？其徒陳元、鄭康成等揚其波，而其學遂盛。及王弼爲注，高談理致，而學者益宗之。然以彖、象、文言參解易爻，使彖、象、文言雜入卦中者，直始之也。故先儒謂古經始變于費氏，而目弼爲老易者，非以其抗高論而衍玄談乎？然經雖變于費氏，而未遺乎經；弼論雖過玄，而經不隨之晦也。迨宋程子作傳，亦惟觀其理，而略于卦畫之分屬。于是朱子本義始集其成，而行于世矣。
書出于史官，羲皇之上，三墳不可
translation_en:
…do not resemble him, and seek someone resembling him among men on the road? Allow me to finish explaining this.

The Changes originated with Fuxi. The Linked Mountains (Lianshan) and Returning to the Hidden (Guicang), the Changes of the Xia and Shang dynasties, can no longer be seen. King Wen appended the hexagram statements, and Confucius composed the texts of the Ten Wings; thus the Changes took its definitive form. Later, because it was used for divination, it escaped burning under the Qin. When the Han arose, the Changes divided into three traditions. Jiao Gan’s Forest of Changes (Yilin) departed from the Way and elaborated numerical schemes, appropriating one aspect while remaining ignorant of the whole; it was certainly no work of a sage. Tian He transmitted it to Zixia [?], obtaining the authentic twelve sections comprising the hexagram images, line statements and judgments, Commentary on the Words, and Explanation of the Trigrams [?]. Although this was the original classic of the Changes, it can no longer be verified today. Was it not Fei Zhi who elaborated its teachings and transmitted them to the present? His followers, Chen Yuan, Zheng Kangcheng, and others, spread its influence, and his school consequently flourished.

When Wang Bi wrote his commentary, he discoursed loftily on principles and their implications, and scholars increasingly took him as their authority. Yet it was Fei Zhi who first used the Judgments, Images, and Commentary on the Words together to explain the lines of the Changes, interspersing these texts within the hexagrams. Thus earlier Confucian scholars said that the ancient classic first underwent alteration at Fei’s hands. And was it not because Wang Bi advanced lofty arguments and elaborated abstruse discourse that they characterized his work as a Laozi-style Changes? Nevertheless, although Fei altered the classic, he did not abandon it; although Wang Bi’s arguments were excessively abstruse, the classic did not thereby become obscure. When Master Cheng of the Song composed his commentary, he too considered only its principles, giving scant attention to the distinctions and affiliations of the hexagram lines. It was only with Master Zhu’s Original Meaning (Benyi) that these achievements were brought together in a synthesis that circulated throughout the world.

The Documents originated with the scribal officials. For the period before the sovereign Fuxi, the Three Ancient Records (Sanfen) cannot…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
見矣孔子斷自堯典迄于秦誓而書成焉
其後燔于秦火漢興而書分爲二伏勝今
文本出耄昏口授之書而謬合之篇艱澀
之語不無外譌之憾古文出自孔壁本孔
惠科斗之傳安國隸古之定而辭皆平易
固爲近之矣然雖盛傳于今而不能無疑
者非以舜典之獨闕耶其後東晉梅賾取
王肅所注今文舜典足其篇而其書始完
及孝明帝更以今文而學者愈便之然伏
===
生離書口授乃盡得其所難而安國考定
于古書磨滅之餘反得其所易此又不可
解者也故宋儒謂訓誥誓命有難易之不
同而不以是槩先秦所引之文豈非以記
錄之語難工而潤色之辭易美乎迨宋蔡
沈授自朱子釋其章句頗爲明悉而古註
疏遂廢矣詩之興也采之列國貢之天王
大子刪之而六義四始于是乎名漢興而
詩分爲四申公訓詁于魯轅固述傳于齊
punctuated:
見矣。孔子斷自堯典，迄于秦誓，而書成焉。其後燔于秦火，漢興而書分爲二。伏勝今文本出耄昏口授之書，而謬合之篇、艱澀之語，不無外譌之憾。古文出自孔壁，本孔惠科斗之傳、安國隸古之定，而辭皆平易，固爲近之矣。然雖盛傳于今，而不能無疑者，非以舜典之獨闕耶？其後東晉梅賾取王肅所注今文舜典足其篇，而其書始完。及孝明帝，更以今文，而學者愈便之。然伏生離書口授，乃盡得其所難，而安國考定于古書磨滅之餘，反得其所易，此又不可解者也。故宋儒謂訓誥誓命有難易之不同，而不以是槩先秦所引之文，豈非以記錄之語難工，而潤色之辭易美乎？迨宋蔡沈授自朱子，釋其章句，頗爲明悉，而古註疏遂廢矣。
詩之興也，采之列國，貢之天王，大子刪之，而六義四始于是乎名。漢興而詩分爲四，申公訓詁于魯，轅固述傳于齊。
translation_en:
…can no longer be seen. Confucius began his selection with the Canon of Yao and ended with the Oath of Qin, thereby compiling the Book of Documents. Later it was burned in the Qin conflagration. With the rise of the Han, the Documents divided into two versions. Fu Sheng’s New Text version originated in a book dictated in the confusion of extreme old age; its erroneously combined chapters and obscure expressions leave grounds for regret over extraneous corruptions. The Old Text emerged from a wall of Confucius’s house. It rested on Kong Hui’s [?] transmission in tadpole script and Kong Anguo’s establishment of the ancient text in clerical script. Its language is uniformly plain and accessible, so it certainly seems closer to the original. Yet although it has circulated widely down to the present, doubts remain: is this not because the Canon of Shun alone was missing? Subsequently, Mei Ze of the Eastern Jin took the New Text Canon of Shun annotated by Wang Su to supply the chapter, and only then was the book complete. Under Emperor Xiaoming, it was further recast in contemporary script, making it still more convenient for students. Yet Master Fu, dictating apart from the written book [?], managed to preserve all the difficult portions, whereas Anguo, critically establishing the text from the remnants of an ancient book whose writing had worn away, instead obtained the easy portions. This, too, is inexplicable. Thus Song scholars said that the instructions, announcements, oaths, and commands differed in difficulty, but did not use this distinction to generalize about the passages quoted before the Qin. Was this not because the language of records is hard to make elegant, while polished wording is readily made beautiful? In the Song, Cai Shen received instruction from Master Zhu and explained the chapters and sentences with considerable clarity and thoroughness; the ancient commentaries and subcommentaries consequently fell out of use.
When the Odes arose, they were collected from the various states and presented to the Son of Heaven. The Crown Prince [?] edited them, and the names of the Six Principles and Four Beginnings were thereby established. With the rise of the Han, the Odes divided into four traditions. Master Shen supplied textual explanations in Lu, and Yuan Gu expounded a commentary in Qi.

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
作內外傳者韓嬰也作詁訓傳者毛萇也
四詩並列學官厥後馬融賈逵鄭康成之
徒皆發揮毛氏而魯齊之詩微矣韓詩僅
存外傳十篇已非全集而其遺論時見于
他書又與經傳不合如關雎正風之首乃
目爲康王政衰之刺詩也謬孰甚焉然則
今日所當表章而考証者舍毛詩奚以哉
而宋儒謂小序非子夏之筆復不滿于毛
萇之所述焉噫作詩微序關雎何以知爲
===
后妃之德也鵲巢何以知爲夫人之德也
雖聖人必不能逆知于千載之上矣毛氏
之祖之也豈果謬耶今集註多宗其所傳
又摘其一二以疵之不亦過乎然綱之以
章句紀之以訓詁察之性情總其領要固
朱子之大功矣禮之教也事爲之制曲爲
之防孔子定之而三千三百于是乎著漢
興而禮出淹中然正禮已亡于諸侯之去
籍雜述各成于孔門之諸子月令有出自
punctuated:
作內外傳者韓嬰也，作詁訓傳者毛萇也。四詩並列學官。厥後馬融、賈逵、鄭康成之徒，皆發揮毛氏，而魯齊之詩微矣。韓詩僅存外傳十篇，已非全集，而其遺論時見于他書，又與經傳不合。如關雎，正風之首，乃目爲康王政衰之刺詩也，謬孰甚焉？然則今日所當表章而考証者，舍毛詩奚以哉？而宋儒謂小序非子夏之筆，復不滿于毛萇之所述焉。噫！作詩微序，關雎何以知爲后妃之德也？鵲巢何以知爲夫人之德也？雖聖人，必不能逆知于千載之上矣。毛氏之祖之也，豈果謬耶？今集註多宗其所傳，又摘其一二以疵之，不亦過乎？然綱之以章句，紀之以訓詁，察之性情，總其領要，固朱子之大功矣。
禮之教也，事爲之制，曲爲之防。孔子定之，而三千三百于是乎著。漢興而禮出淹中，然正禮已亡于諸侯之去籍，雜述各成于孔門之諸子。月令有出自
translation_en:
…Han Ying composed the Inner and Outer Commentaries, and Mao Chang composed the Explanations and Glosses. All four traditions of the Odes were established in the official schools. Subsequently, Ma Rong, Jia Kui, Zheng Kangcheng, and others elucidated the Mao tradition, while the Lu and Qi traditions declined. Of Han’s Odes, only the ten chapters of the Outer Commentary survive; this is no longer the complete collection. Its surviving interpretations also appear occasionally in other books, yet they disagree with the classic and its commentaries. For example, “Guanju,” the first of the orthodox Airs, is actually designated a poem criticizing the decline of government under King Kang. What error could be greater? Thus, what should we honor, promote, and critically examine today, if not Mao’s Odes? Yet Song scholars maintained that the Lesser Prefaces were not written by Zixia and were also dissatisfied with Mao Chang’s account. Alas! Without the prefaces explaining the composition of the poems, how could we know that “Guanju” concerns the virtue of the royal consort, or that “Quechao” concerns the virtue of a feudal lord’s wife? Even a sage surely could not know retrospectively what lay a thousand years in the past. Was Mao really mistaken in taking these prefaces as his foundation? The present Collected Commentaries largely follows what he transmitted, yet singles out one or two points to criticize. Is this not excessive? Nevertheless, to organize the text through divisions into chapters and sentences, order it through explanatory glosses, examine its human dispositions and feelings, and draw together its essential meaning—these are indeed Master Zhu’s great achievements.
As for the teaching of ritual, it establishes regulations for every affair and safeguards for every particular. Confucius fixed it, and thus the three thousand minor rules and three hundred major rules became manifest. With the rise of the Han, texts on ritual emerged from Yanzhong. Yet the orthodox rites had already been lost when the feudal lords discarded their records, while miscellaneous accounts were separately compiled by Confucius’s disciples. As for the “Monthly Ordinances,” there is a view that it originated with…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
公孫尼子之疑也王制有作于呂不韋之
疑也后蒼傳魯高堂生所授禮十七篇厥
後戴德戴聖慶普之徒皆闡明之又共爲
補綴得百餘篇由是三家俱列于學官矣
三鄭王肅諸人爲之註訓雖各精其學而
說多不同如閒居燕居表紀緇衣自成一
書而小康之嘆德怨之報又涉于老氏則
夫今日所當釐正而宗主者舍儀禮曷以
哉宋儒謂宜以儀禮爲經禮記爲傳而致
===
望于當時焉其說謂儀禮有冠禮二記有
冠義儀禮有婚禮禮記有婚義至燕射之
類莫不皆然況韓昌黎讀儀禮亦謂文王
周公之法制在于是耶今觀陳灝之註禮
記也于其舛且謬矣未嘗不指而駁之所
見不亦同乎然風傳俗習裔制蝕器禮賴
以猶存後因之可考諸子則信非附會矣
若夫孔子春秋之作尊王賤伯內華外夷
將以正誼明道章往考來也故言高而旨
punctuated:
公孫尼子之疑也，王制有作于呂不韋之疑也。后蒼傳魯高堂生所授禮十七篇，厥後戴德、戴聖、慶普之徒皆闡明之，又共爲補綴，得百餘篇，由是三家俱列于學官矣。三鄭、王肅諸人爲之註訓，雖各精其學，而說多不同。如閒居、燕居、表紀、緇衣，自成一書，而小康之嘆、德怨之報，又涉于老氏，則夫今日所當釐正而宗主者，舍儀禮曷以哉？宋儒謂宜以儀禮爲經，禮記爲傳，而致望于當時焉。其說謂儀禮有冠禮，二記有冠義；儀禮有婚禮，禮記有婚義；至燕射之類，莫不皆然。況韓昌黎讀儀禮，亦謂文王、周公之法制在于是耶？今觀陳灝之註禮記也，于其舛且謬矣，未嘗不指而駁之，所見不亦同乎？然風傳俗習，裔制蝕器，禮賴以猶存，後因之可考諸子，則信非附會矣。

若夫孔子春秋之作，尊王賤伯，內華外夷，將以正誼明道，章往考來也。故言高而旨
translation_en:
…there is doubt as to whether it was by Gongsun Nizi; likewise, there is doubt as to whether “Royal Regulations” was composed by Lü Buwei. Hou Cang transmitted the seventeen chapters on ritual taught by Master Gaotang of Lu. Subsequently, Dai De, Dai Sheng, Qing Pu, and their followers all elucidated them and jointly supplemented and pieced them together, obtaining over a hundred chapters. Thus all three schools were established in the official educational institutions. The three Zhengs [?], Wang Su, and others supplied commentaries and explanations. Although each was accomplished in this learning, their interpretations frequently differed. Chapters such as “At Leisure,” “At Ease,” “Record of Exemplary Conduct” [?], and “Black Robes” each constitute a work in their own right; yet the lament over Lesser Tranquillity and the discussion of repaying kindness and resentment also touch upon the teachings of Laozi. If we are to rectify these matters today and establish an authoritative basis, what could we use other than the Ceremonies and Rites (Yili)? Song Confucians argued that the Ceremonies and Rites should serve as the canonical text and the Record of Rites (Liji) as its commentary, and placed their hopes in the men of their own time. Their explanation was that the Ceremonies and Rites contains the capping ceremony, while the “two records” [?] contain “The Meaning of the Capping Ceremony”; the Ceremonies and Rites contains the marriage ceremony, while the Record of Rites contains “The Meaning of the Marriage Ceremony.” The same holds for banqueting, archery, and the like. Moreover, when Han Changli read the Ceremonies and Rites, did he not also say that the institutions of King Wen and the Duke of Zhou were preserved therein? Looking now at Chen Hao’s commentary on the Record of Rites, we find that he invariably identifies and refutes its inconsistencies and errors. Is his understanding not the same? Nevertheless, through transmitted customs and habitual practices, inherited institutions and worn ritual vessels [?], ritual still survives. Later generations can use these to examine the writings of the various masters; thus these are indeed no mere contrived associations.

As for Confucius’s composition of the Spring and Autumn Annals, it exalts kings and disparages hegemons, treats the Hua as insiders and the Yi as outsiders, intending thereby to set right righteousness, illuminate the Way, make the past manifest, and scrutinize what is to come. Thus its language is lofty and its purport…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
遠辭約而義微學之而能極其說者鮮矣
鄒夾最微漢巳無傳明其說而並傳至今
者非左氏公羊穀梁乎然三氏之說所見
互異如齊人歸田滕子來朝與墮三都之
類是也古謂左氏以當世之見決當世之
事事雖詳而義鄙公穀傳聞率多謬誤辭
未鄭重情雖踈而明道宋儒胡氏參伍以
定之愽其旨趣闔闢有條而不無牽强之
議是將安所從乎今觀左氏之文也或先
===
經以始事或後經以終義或依經以辯理
或錯經以合異非窺聖道信嚮不如是之
篤非身見國史本末不如是之詳舍之益
荒謬矣以之爲案不亦可乎嗚呼方輿異
言履其地者定輕重匿形懸其權者分不
志于聖人無以知其言也不知其言而能
辯物者寡矣諸子固非知聖人之道者然
謂之不志于聖人之道不可也六經之文
缺譌雖有間矣近古者不猶得其音塵哉
punctuated: 遠，辭約而義微，學之而能極其說者鮮矣。鄒、夾最微，漢巳無傳。明其說而並傳至今者，非左氏、公羊、穀梁乎？然三氏之說，所見互異，如齊人歸田、滕子來朝與墮三都之類是也。古謂左氏以當世之見決當世之事，事雖詳而義鄙；公、穀傳聞率多謬誤，辭未鄭重，情雖踈而明道。宋儒胡氏參伍以定之，愽其旨趣，闔闢有條，而不無牽强之議，是將安所從乎？今觀左氏之文也，或先經以始事，或後經以終義，或依經以辯理，或錯經以合異。非窺聖道，信嚮不如是之篤；非身見國史，本末不如是之詳。舍之益荒謬矣，以之爲案，不亦可乎？嗚呼！方輿異言，履其地者定；輕重匿形，懸其權者分。不志于聖人，無以知其言也；不知其言而能辯物者寡矣。諸子固非知聖人之道者，然謂之不志于聖人之道，不可也。六經之文，缺譌雖有間矣，近古者不猶得其音塵哉！
translation_en: …far-reaching in purport, concise in wording, and subtle in meaning; few who study it can fully fathom its teachings. The Zou and Jia traditions were the most obscure, and by the Han dynasty they were no longer transmitted. Was it not the Zuo, Gongyang, and Guliang commentaries that elucidated its teachings and have all been transmitted to the present? Yet the views of these three commentaries differ from one another, as in their accounts of the people of Qi returning fields, the lord of Teng coming to court, and the demolition of the three fortified capitals. It was said of old that Zuo judged the affairs of his own age through the understanding of that age: although detailed in recording events, his interpretation was shallow. The Gongyang and Guliang accounts, based on hearsay, contain numerous errors; their wording lacks due gravity [?], and although their accounts of circumstances are sketchy, they illuminate the Way. The Song Confucian scholar Hu compared and cross-checked them to establish his interpretations, elaborating their purport and arranging his exposition methodically. Yet he has not escaped criticism for strained interpretations. Which, then, should one follow? Now, examining Zuo’s text, we find that it sometimes precedes the Classic to introduce an event, sometimes follows the Classic to complete its meaning, sometimes follows the Classic to elucidate principles, and sometimes interweaves passages from the Classic to reconcile differences. Had he not glimpsed the Way of the Sage, his faith and devotion could not have been so firm; had he not personally seen the histories of the states, his account of events from beginning to end could not have been so detailed. To discard it would lead to still greater error. Would it not be acceptable to use it as the basis for judgment? Alas! When accounts of geography differ, those who have traversed the terrain settle the matter; when relative weight is hidden from view, those who suspend a balance distinguish it. Without setting one’s mind upon the Sage, one has no means of understanding his words; and few can distinguish things properly without understanding his words. These masters were certainly not people who fully understood the Way of the Sage, yet it would be wrong to say that they did not aspire to it. Although gaps and corruptions occur here and there in the texts of the Six Classics, did not those who lived nearer to antiquity still catch echoes and traces of it?

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
是故易廣矣大矣爻象可一一而拘之耶
本之王弼而會之程傳本義斯不泥乎書
精矣微矣獨見能一一而盡之耶主之以
孔傳而參之以諸䟽蔡註斯盡善乎小序
說詩之祖也舍毛詩則莫之考矣誦朱傳
而參之序焉可也儀禮實踐之文也朱子
註之謂有小補于世矣經儀禮而列記爲
傳焉可也若夫春秋旣以左氏爲案則參
之以公穀會之以胡氏不亦免于虛且臆
===
之罪耶故曰茂木之叢多美材焉獨鳴之
鳥寡和音焉闕疑識大之學願有望于稽
古明經之士也狂僻之見如斯敢贅陳以
就正于執事
第三問
楊吉
同考試官教諭魏　批〔吏治之卑弊在遷代速而德教薄知其弊而善反之僅見此篇〕
考試官教諭盧　批〔援古證今卓有定論他日服官〕
punctuated:
是故《易》廣矣，大矣，爻象可一一而拘之耶？本之王弼，而會之《程傳》《本義》，斯不泥乎？《書》精矣，微矣，獨見能一一而盡之耶？主之以《孔傳》，而參之以諸䟽、蔡註，斯盡善乎？《小序》，說《詩》之祖也，舍《毛詩》則莫之考矣。誦《朱傳》而參之《序》焉，可也。《儀禮》，實踐之文也。朱子註之，謂有小補于世矣。經《儀禮》而列《記》爲傳焉，可也。若夫《春秋》，旣以《左氏》爲案，則參之以《公》《穀》，會之以胡氏，不亦免于虛且臆之罪耶？故曰：茂木之叢，多美材焉；獨鳴之鳥，寡和音焉。闕疑識大之學，願有望于稽古明經之士也。狂僻之見如斯，敢贅陳以就正于執事。
第三問
楊吉
同考試官教諭魏，批〔吏治之卑，弊在遷代速而德教薄。知其弊而善反之，僅見此篇。〕
考試官教諭盧，批〔援古證今，卓有定論。他日服官〕
translation_en:
Thus the Book of Changes is broad and great: can its line statements and images each be confined to a fixed interpretation? Taking Wang Bi as the foundation and bringing his interpretation together with Cheng’s Commentary and the Original Meaning, would one not avoid rigid adherence? The Book of Documents is refined and subtle: can a single person’s insights exhaust every aspect of it? Taking Kong’s Commentary as the principal guide and consulting the various subcommentaries and Cai’s commentary alongside it, would one not attain a fully sound understanding? The Lesser Prefaces are the foundation of interpretation of the Book of Odes; without the Mao recension of the Odes, there would be no way to investigate them. It is acceptable to recite Zhu’s Commentary and consult the Prefaces alongside it. The Ceremonies and Rites is a text for actual practice. Master Zhu annotated it, saying that it would offer some small benefit to the world. It is acceptable to treat the Ceremonies and Rites as the classic and to rank the Record of Rites as its commentary. As for the Spring and Autumn Annals, once Zuo’s Commentary is taken as the basis, would consulting the Gongyang and Guliang commentaries and bringing them together with Hu’s commentary not avert the fault of empty speculation? Thus it is said: among luxuriant trees there is much fine timber; a bird singing alone finds few answering voices. For learning that leaves doubtful matters unresolved while grasping the essentials, I would place my hopes in scholars who investigate antiquity and understand the classics. Such are my rash and eccentric views; I venture to set them out at length for your correction.
Third Question
Yang Ji
Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor, comments: 〔The decline in local administration stems from excessively rapid replacement of officials and inadequate moral instruction. This is the only essay I have seen that recognizes these defects and aptly proposes their remedy.〕
Examiner Lu, Instructor, comments: 〔Drawing on antiquity to substantiate arguments about the present, this essay offers remarkably firm conclusions. When he holds office in the future …〕

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
是必以循良稱者
考試官學正丘　批　有用之學
馭守令之道在重久任以責其成崇德化
以正其習而已夫道久化成帝王所以長
世以德化民循良所以培植國脉者也任
弗久則苟且遷延之政行化弗崇則簿書
期會之責塞雖欲言治皆苟而已明主知
其然以久任爲馭吏之權以德化爲倡導
之機鼓舞於廟堂之上而風行於海宇之
===
廣運是道焉耳孔子曰道之以政齊之以
刑民免而無耻道之以德齊之以禮有耻
且格言政刑不如德化也董仲舒曰守令
者民之師帥言師帥以教導之帥以督率之
兼治教之責者也今之守令顧急於刑而
緩於德棄師道而專以督率爲事何哉是
故崇德化以漸漬之所以正其習也重久
任以優游之所以定其志也習正而俗吏
之患袪志定而天下之治成矣昔三代盛
punctuated:
是必以循良稱者。
考試官學正丘　批：有用之學。
馭守令之道，在重久任以責其成，崇德化以正其習而已。夫道久化成，帝王所以長世；以德化民，循良所以培植國脉者也。任弗久，則苟且遷延之政行；化弗崇，則簿書期會之責塞。雖欲言治，皆苟而已。明主知其然，以久任爲馭吏之權，以德化爲倡導之機，鼓舞於廟堂之上，而風行於海宇之廣，運是道焉耳。孔子曰：「道之以政，齊之以刑，民免而無耻；道之以德，齊之以禮，有耻且格。」言政刑不如德化也。董仲舒曰：「守令者，民之師帥。」言師帥以教導之，帥以督率之，兼治教之責者也。今之守令，顧急於刑而緩於德，棄師道而專以督率爲事，何哉？是故崇德化以漸漬之，所以正其習也；重久任以優游之，所以定其志也。習正而俗吏之患袪，志定而天下之治成矣。昔三代盛
translation_en:
…this is surely someone who will win renown as a conscientious and benevolent official.
Examiner Qiu, School Director, comments: Learning of practical use.
The way to govern prefects and county magistrates consists simply in valuing long tenure so as to hold them accountable for results, and in honoring moral transformation so as to rectify their habits. By sustaining the Way until its transforming influence is complete, emperors and kings make their dynasties endure; by transforming the people through virtue, conscientious and benevolent officials nourish the lifeblood of the state. If tenure is not long, expedient and dilatory administration prevails; if moral transformation is not honored, officials merely discharge their obligations concerning documents and deadlines. Even if they wish to speak of good government, everything remains a matter of expediency. Understanding this, an enlightened ruler uses long tenure as a means of governing officials and moral transformation as the means of inspiring and guiding them. He encourages them from the imperial court, and his influence spreads like the wind throughout the vast realm: he simply puts this Way into practice. Confucius said: “Guide them through administrative measures and bring them into line through punishments, and the people will evade punishment but have no sense of shame. Guide them through virtue and bring them into line through ritual, and they will have a sense of shame and moreover reform themselves.” This means that administrative measures and punishments are inferior to moral transformation. Dong Zhongshu said: “Prefects and county magistrates are the teachers and leaders of the people.” This means that, as teachers and leaders, they instruct and guide them [?], and as leaders they supervise and direct them, bearing responsibility for both government and education. Yet today’s prefects and county magistrates are zealous about punishment and remiss about virtue. Why do they abandon the teacher’s way and make supervision and direction their sole concern? Thus, honoring moral transformation so that its influence gradually permeates them is the means of rectifying their habits; valuing long tenure so that they have time and ease to carry out their duties is the means of steadying their resolve. Once their habits are rectified, the troubles caused by commonplace officials are dispelled; once their resolve is steady, good government throughout the realm is achieved. Formerly, in the flourishing age of the Three Dynasties…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
時純任德教上下相親淳風沕穆弗可尚
已自有郡縣以來英君誼辟嘉三代之治
慕隆古之化者曷可勝數率駁而不純格
而弗遇所鼓舞倡導者非其機也漢興除
秦煩苛與民更始文景清靜恭儉愛養元
元七十餘年之間網疏而民富家給而人
足人自愛而重犯法先行義而後絀辱人
知文景富而知教矣不知其以德化民既
能正其習居官長子孫又能定其志故風
===
移俗易比隆成康也當是時吏皆循良安
有循良之名乎逮乎建元求平之間法理
之士咸精其能競爲苛刻以避誅責民輕
犯法俗流世壞由是文翁興學於成都黃
霸宣德於潁川龔遂化盜於渤海信臣興
利於南陽倪寬以課最稱卓茂以寬仁著
魯恭以三異顯張堪以兩岐謠廉范以五
袴歌布美化於當時表循良於列傳迨景
星麟鳳之希闊矣百五十年俗吏離散民
punctuated: 時，純任德教，上下相親，淳風沕穆，弗可尚已。自有郡縣以來，英君誼辟嘉三代之治、慕隆古之化者，曷可勝數？率駁而不純，格而弗遇，所鼓舞倡導者非其機也。漢興，除秦煩苛，與民更始。文景清靜恭儉，愛養元元。七十餘年之間，網疏而民富，家給而人足，人自愛而重犯法，先行義而後絀辱。人知文景富而知教矣，不知其以德化民，既能正其習，居官長子孫，又能定其志，故風移俗易，比隆成康也。當是時，吏皆循良，安有循良之名乎？逮乎建元求平之間，法理之士咸精其能，競爲苛刻，以避誅責。民輕犯法，俗流世壞。由是文翁興學於成都，黃霸宣德於潁川，龔遂化盜於渤海，信臣興利於南陽，倪寬以課最稱，卓茂以寬仁著，魯恭以三異顯，張堪以兩岐謠，廉范以五袴歌，布美化於當時，表循良於列傳，迨景星麟鳳之希闊矣。百五十年，俗吏離散民
translation_en:
… in those times, they relied entirely on moral instruction. Those above and below were close to one another, and their pure customs were profound and harmonious, beyond all surpassing. Since commanderies and counties were established, how could one count all the enlightened rulers and righteous sovereigns who admired the government of the Three Dynasties and yearned for the transforming influence of high antiquity? Yet their achievements were generally mixed rather than pure, obstructed rather than fulfilled: what they encouraged and promoted did not address the essential workings of government.

When the Han arose, it abolished the Qin’s burdensome and harsh measures and made a fresh beginning with the people. Emperors Wen and Jing governed with tranquility, reverence, and frugality, cherishing and nourishing the common people. Over more than seventy years, the net of the law was loose, yet the people prospered; households had enough, and individuals wanted for nothing. People respected themselves and regarded breaking the law as a grave matter; they put righteous conduct first and disgrace last. People know that Wen and Jing brought prosperity and understood moral instruction, but they do not understand that, by transforming the people through virtue, these emperors corrected their habits, while allowing officials to remain in office long enough to raise children and grandchildren also gave stability to their purposes. Thus prevailing habits and customs changed, and their flourishing government rivaled that of Kings Cheng and Kang. At that time, all officials were conscientious and good: what need was there for a special designation of ‘conscientious and good officials’?

By the period between Jianyuan and Qiuping [?], specialists in legal administration had all honed their skills and competed in harshness to avoid punishment and censure. The people thought little of breaking the law, customs deteriorated, and society fell into disorder. Against this background, Wen Weng promoted learning in Chengdu; Huang Ba spread virtuous influence in Yingchuan; Gong Sui reformed bandits in Bohai; and Xinchen developed projects benefiting the people in Nanyang. Ni Kuan [?] was praised for receiving the highest performance assessment; Zhuo Mao was renowned for generosity and benevolence; Lu Gong became distinguished through three extraordinary portents; Zhang Kan was celebrated in a ballad about grain bearing double ears; and Lian Fan was praised in the song of the ‘five pairs of trousers.’ They spread beneficial moral influence in their own times and were singled out as conscientious and good officials in the collected biographies. They were nearly [?] as rare as auspicious stars, qilin, and phoenixes. For a hundred and fifty years, vulgar officials alienated the people …

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
心斲喪元氣豈少也哉蓋由當時專尚法
制既非化民之本數易守宰又非久任之
道良吏雖盛安能如文景之淳厚哉觀於
章帝詔戒苛刻忠厚惻怛懇懇然溢於言
表當時吏治可知矣宋人有言在位者數
徙則上不能狃習而知其事下不肯服馴
而安其教賢者功不可以及其成不肖者
罪未至於著若夫迎新將故之勞緣絕簿
書之弊固其害之小者嗚呼久任責成崇
化正習眞帝王馭吏之要乎我
===
明稽古定制內外官率三年一考六年再考不
稱職者復其職以冀後効俟九年通考然
後黜陟行焉外官善政著聞即旌異之秩
滿者增秩仍其舊任即久任責成之法也
有
大誥三編敎民榜文爲善陰騭資世通訓等書
頒布天下家習人誦即崇尚德化之意也
百餘年間吏治安靜民物熈恬仕者無奔
punctuated:
心，斲喪元氣，豈少也哉？蓋由當時專尚法制，既非化民之本；數易守宰，又非久任之道。良吏雖盛，安能如文景之淳厚哉？觀於章帝詔戒苛刻，忠厚惻怛，懇懇然溢於言表，當時吏治可知矣。宋人有言：「在位者數徙，則上不能狃習而知其事，下不肯服馴而安其教。賢者功不可以及其成，不肖者罪未至於著。若夫迎新將故之勞，緣絕簿書之弊，固其害之小者。」嗚呼！久任責成，崇化正習，眞帝王馭吏之要乎！

我明稽古定制，內外官率三年一考，六年再考。不稱職者復其職，以冀後効；俟九年通考，然後黜陟行焉。外官善政著聞，即旌異之；秩滿者增秩，仍其舊任，即久任責成之法也。有《大誥》三編、《敎民榜文》、《爲善陰騭》、《資世通訓》等書，頒布天下，家習人誦，即崇尚德化之意也。百餘年間，吏治安靜，民物熈恬，仕者無奔
translation_en:
…the people's hearts, and sapped the vital energies of the realm—was the damage slight? This arose because exclusive esteem was then given to laws and regulations, which were not the foundation for transforming the people, while prefects and magistrates were frequently replaced, contrary to the principle of keeping officials long in office. Although good officials were numerous, how could conditions have matched the simple goodness of the reigns of Emperors Wen and Jing? Consider Emperor Zhang's edict warning against harshness: sincerity, generosity, and compassion earnestly overflowed its words. From this one can understand the state of official administration at the time. A writer of the Song said: “When officeholders are frequently transferred, those above cannot become accustomed to their duties and understand their work, while those below are unwilling to submit willingly and find contentment in their instruction. The worthy cannot bring their achievements to completion, and the offenses of the unworthy have not yet become apparent. As for the toil of welcoming new officials and seeing off their predecessors, and the disruption of administrative records [?], these are merely the lesser harms.” Alas! Keeping officials long in office and holding them responsible for results, honoring moral transformation and rectifying customary practices—are these not truly the essentials by which emperors and kings govern their officials?

Our Ming dynasty consulted antiquity in establishing its institutions. Officials in the capital and outside it generally undergo an evaluation after three years and a second after six. Those who prove unequal to their duties are restored to their posts in the hope that they will subsequently render effective service. Only after a comprehensive evaluation at nine years are demotions and promotions carried out. Officials outside the capital whose good administration becomes widely known are singled out for commendation. Those who complete their terms receive an increase in rank while remaining in their existing posts. This is precisely the method of keeping officials long in office and holding them responsible for results. Such works as the three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements (Da Gao), Placards for Instructing the People (Jiaomin Bangwen), Doing Good and Hidden Blessings (Weishan Yinzhi), and Comprehensive Instructions to Aid the World (Zishi Tongxun) have been promulgated throughout the realm, studied in every household and recited by everyone. This embodies the intention to esteem transformation through virtue. For more than a hundred years, official administration has been peaceful and orderly, and the people and all things have flourished in tranquility; those serving in office have been spared the toil of rushing…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
走之勞閭閻鮮愁嘆之聲庶幾乎成康文
景之治矣邇年以來選法壅滯少變其初
守令視官府爲傳舍百姓爲秦越甫及一
考卽興淹滯之嘆矣以德化爲迂闊速化
爲捷徑簿書期會之餘他弗遑恤矣俗漸
流失習漸敗壞挽淳風以倡鼓舞之機不
有在於此時乎玆欲復久任之法必先明
立條格頒布天下俾爲守令者安其位而
定其志毋奔兢躁進毋謟諛黷貨三年一
===
考量加之祿六年再考量增之秩有善政
則賜璽書以褒美俟九年報政破常格以
超遷或晉以卿寺之階或錫以崇品之服
如漢之褰帷行郡增秩賜金則守令不病
於久任矣若病其迂滯難行試質以弘治
成化間猶有州守擢府守府守擢京卿九
載加秩仍復舊任者奚取法於異代乎欲
崇德化必先申明禮教風示郡邑毋爲察
察之明毋尚赫赫之政敦尚孝悌廉恥之
punctuated:
走之勞，閭閻鮮愁嘆之聲，庶幾乎成康文景之治矣。邇年以來，選法壅滯，少變其初。守令視官府爲傳舍，百姓爲秦越，甫及一考，卽興淹滯之嘆矣。以德化爲迂闊，速化爲捷徑，簿書期會之餘，他弗遑恤矣。俗漸流失，習漸敗壞，挽淳風以倡鼓舞之機，不有在於此時乎？
玆欲復久任之法，必先明立條格，頒布天下，俾爲守令者安其位而定其志，毋奔兢躁進，毋謟諛黷貨。三年一考，量加之祿；六年再考，量增之秩。有善政，則賜璽書以褒美。俟九年報政，破常格以超遷，或晉以卿寺之階，或錫以崇品之服。如漢之褰帷行郡、增秩賜金，則守令不病於久任矣。若病其迂滯難行，試質以弘治成化間，猶有州守擢府守、府守擢京卿、九載加秩仍復舊任者，奚取法於異代乎？
欲崇德化，必先申明禮教，風示郡邑，毋爲察察之明，毋尚赫赫之政，敦尚孝悌廉恥之
translation_en:
…the toil of rushing about, while in the villages one seldom heard cries of sorrow or lamentation. This came close to the good government of Kings Cheng and Kang of Zhou and Emperors Wen and Jing of Han. In recent years, however, the system of official selection has become obstructed, departing somewhat from its original form. Prefects and magistrates regard their offices as travelers’ lodgings and the common people as strangers as distant as Qin and Yue. Barely have they reached their first evaluation before they begin lamenting their stalled advancement. They consider transformation through moral virtue impractical and rapid transformation a shortcut. Beyond registers, documents, deadlines, and reporting requirements, they have no time to attend to anything else. Customs steadily go astray, and habits steadily deteriorate. Is this not precisely the moment to restore wholesome customs and set encouragement and inspiration in motion?
If we now wish to restore the practice of long tenure, we must first establish clear regulations and promulgate them throughout the realm, so that prefects and magistrates may feel secure in their posts and settled in their purpose. They must not scramble for advancement or seek it impatiently, nor engage in flattery or corrupt acquisition of wealth. At their first evaluation after three years, their stipends should be increased as appropriate; at their second evaluation after six years, their ranks should be raised as appropriate. Those who govern well should receive letters bearing the imperial seal in commendation. When they report on their administration after nine years, ordinary rules should be set aside to grant exceptional promotion: some should be advanced to the ranks of chief ministers of court agencies, others awarded the robes of high rank. Follow the Han examples of lifting the carriage curtains while touring a commandery, raising officials’ ranks, and awarding gold; then prefects and magistrates will not find long tenure burdensome. If anyone objects that this is cumbersome and difficult to implement, consider that even during the Hongzhi and Chenghua reigns, department magistrates were promoted to prefects, prefects to chief ministers at the capital, and officials who had served nine years received higher rank while remaining in their former posts. Why seek models in another dynasty?
To promote transformation through moral virtue, we must first reaffirm ritual instruction and make it an example for the commanderies and counties. Officials must not display their discernment through minute scrutiny, nor prize conspicuously stern government. They should earnestly esteem the conduct of filial piety, fraternal deference, integrity, and a sense of shame…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
行作興里社庠序之敎督之以勸而匡其
不逮行之以漸而竢其自化如文翁之在
蜀黃霸之治潁川務愷悌廉平之習鷙悍
陰酷之戒則德化不患其不行矣若病其
迂闊難行試質以通訓等書布在方冊里
社庠校遍滿天下者果何爲乎雖然久任
可矣內外輕重之勢不可以不均今之列
京職者以外補爲左遷處郡邑者以親民
爲卑辱若權其重輕均其勞逸更迭出入
===
如唐制官人之法無軒輊過甚則守令重
而久任可行矣崇尚敎化得矣寬假便宜
之權不可以不行今學古之士或短於簿
書卓犖之才或苦於文法苟優以便宜隆
以體貌如漢時褒旌之典俾得從容展布
則守令尊而德化可流矣泥古之士學未
通今狂斐之言罔知忌諱唯執事進而敎
之幸甚
第四問
punctuated:
行，作興里社庠序之敎，督之以勸而匡其不逮，行之以漸而竢其自化。如文翁之在蜀、黃霸之治潁川，務愷悌廉平之習、鷙悍陰酷之戒，則德化不患其不行矣。若病其迂闊難行，試質以《通訓》等書布在方冊，里社庠校遍滿天下者，果何爲乎？雖然，久任可矣，內外輕重之勢不可以不均。今之列京職者，以外補爲左遷；處郡邑者，以親民爲卑辱。若權其重輕，均其勞逸，更迭出入，如唐制官人之法，無軒輊過甚，則守令重而久任可行矣。崇尚敎化得矣，寬假便宜之權不可以不行。今學古之士，或短於簿書；卓犖之才，或苦於文法。苟優以便宜，隆以體貌，如漢時褒旌之典，俾得從容展布，則守令尊而德化可流矣。泥古之士，學未通今，狂斐之言，罔知忌諱，唯執事進而敎之，幸甚。

第四問
translation_en:
…conduct, and invigorate instruction in village communities and local schools. Spur the people on with encouragement and correct their shortcomings; proceed gradually and await their transformation of their own accord. Follow Wen Weng in Shu and Huang Ba in his administration of Yingchuan: cultivate habits of kindness, integrity, and fairness, and guard against ferocity and covert cruelty. Then there need be no fear that moral transformation will fail to take effect. If this is thought impractical and difficult to carry out, consider this: for what purpose, then, do such books as General Instructions (Tongxun) exist in written form, and village communities and local schools fill the realm?

Nevertheless, while long tenure is desirable, the relative standing of service at court and in the provinces must be balanced. Those now holding capital posts regard appointment outside the capital as a demotion; those serving in prefectures and counties regard governing the people directly as lowly and humiliating. If the relative standing of these posts were weighed, their burdens and ease balanced, and officials rotated between service within and outside the capital, following the Tang system of official appointments, without excessive disparities in status, then prefects and magistrates would gain standing, and long tenure could be put into practice.

To esteem moral instruction is right, but officials must also be granted latitude and discretionary authority. Scholars versed in antiquity may be deficient in paperwork, while men of outstanding talent may be hampered by administrative rules. If they were favored with discretion and accorded dignified treatment, following the Han precedents for commendation and distinction, so that they could exercise their abilities freely, then prefects and magistrates would be respected and moral transformation could spread.

I am a scholar bound to antiquity, whose learning has yet to comprehend the present. In these rash and ill-considered words, I have taken no account of taboos. I would be most fortunate if you, honored examiners, would guide and instruct me.

Fourth Question

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
劉希臯
同考試官教諭蔡　批〔權衡古人輕重不爽末復進之三代之前可以觀尚友之志矣〕
考試官教諭盧　批〔才氣雄渾議論精確定低昻乎取舍之閒是策之擅塲者〕
考試官學正丘　批〔有識見〕
考古人之所建立者惟當取其大節要古
人之所成就者則當歸諸盡善夫致治戡
亂務學亮節卓然有所建立者皆君子之
===
偉行論世者所宜亟稱奚暇究其餘也至
於要其成就則庸言細行小過不及皆聖
人之所責備者是則不容於無所歸矣知
此則我雍土漢唐而下先哲炳然大節可
觀者固均非所敢誣然而醇乎其中要之
不詭於聖人者又當表而極言之也孰事
以關隴人物下詢承學蓋欲觀其尚友之
志也敢不掇所聞以復崧高之詩曰維嶽
降神生甫及申言山河之靈往往鍾人出
punctuated:
劉希臯

同考試官教諭蔡，批〔權衡古人，輕重不爽。末復進之三代之前，可以觀尚友之志矣。〕

考試官教諭盧，批〔才氣雄渾，議論精確，定低昻乎取舍之閒，是策之擅塲者。〕

考試官學正丘，批〔有識見。〕

考古人之所建立者，惟當取其大節；要古人之所成就者，則當歸諸盡善。夫致治戡亂、務學亮節，卓然有所建立者，皆君子之偉行。論世者所宜亟稱，奚暇究其餘也？至於要其成就，則庸言細行、小過不及，皆聖人之所責備者，是則不容於無所歸矣。知此，則我雍土漢唐而下先哲，炳然大節可觀者，固均非所敢誣；然而醇乎其中，要之不詭於聖人者，又當表而極言之也。孰事以關隴人物下詢承學，蓋欲觀其尚友之志也。敢不掇所聞以復？《崧高》之詩曰：「維嶽降神，生甫及申。」言山河之靈，往往鍾人出
translation_en:
Liu Xigao

Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor, comments: 〔He weighs the ancients without error in assigning their relative worth. At the end, he reaches further back to the time before the Three Dynasties, revealing his aspiration to befriend the worthy of antiquity.〕

Examiner Lu, Instructor, comments: 〔His talent and spirit are powerful and ample, his arguments precise. In accepting and rejecting, he determines relative merit: he is an outstanding practitioner of the policy essay.〕

Examiner Qiu, School Director, comments: 〔He has discernment.〕

In examining what the ancients established, we should attend above all to their conduct in matters of great principle; in assessing their ultimate attainments, however, we should hold them to the standard of complete goodness. Bringing about good government and suppressing disorder, applying oneself to learning and displaying integrity—these outstanding achievements are all noble deeds of exemplary men. Those who judge past ages should praise them readily; what leisure have they to probe everything else? Yet when assessing their ultimate attainments, ordinary words and minor actions, small faults and shortcomings, are all things in which the sage demands perfection. Here one cannot dispense with an ultimate standard. Understanding this, we certainly dare not misrepresent any of the earlier worthies of our land of Yong, from the Han and Tang onward, whose great integrity shines forth for all to see. Yet those among them who were pure, and whose conduct, taken as a whole, did not depart from the sages, deserve especially to be singled out and praised to the fullest. Your honor [?], in condescending to question us students about the figures of Guan and Long, presumably wishes to discern our aspiration to befriend the worthy of antiquity. How could I fail to gather what I have heard and offer a reply? The ode “Lofty Mountains” (Song gao) says: “The sacred peaks sent down their spirit, giving birth to Fu and Shen.” This means that the spiritual potency of mountains and rivers often concentrates in people who emerge …

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
爲彥聖也維關陝爲古雍州形勝甲於天
下華嶽終南苞其靈黃河涇渭衍其秀故
發而爲聖爲賢者詩書所稱無容論矣其
他多才多藝歷代紛紛亦姑舍是試舉漢
唐而下明問所及者言之彼大臣宗子之
家相所賴以調元贊化者也雍之相業有
若總領衆職之魏相焉去壅蔽而力諫匈
奴之伐和陰陽而屢陳災異之狀知大體
之丙吉遇其配也故稱之者曰丙魏有聲
===
顧不偉與有若裁處無滯之杜如晦焉衆
帷幄而剖決如流官臺閣而規模創定善
謀之房玄齡資其斷也故賢之者曰前有
房杜顧不美與守正不阿嘗見推於宋璟
峭直不避復見重於明皇天下必肥此韓
休所以忠於唐也忠義兼資首建親征之
策忘身徇國恥爲城下之盟澶淵却狄此
寇準所以顯於宋也之四公者功在社稷
而澤潤生民相業之表著不有光於西土
punctuated:
爲彥聖也。維關陝爲古雍州，形勝甲於天下。華嶽、終南苞其靈，黃河、涇渭衍其秀，故發而爲聖爲賢者，詩書所稱，無容論矣。其他多才多藝，歷代紛紛，亦姑舍是。試舉漢唐而下明問所及者言之。
彼大臣，宗子之家相，所賴以調元贊化者也。雍之相業，有若總領衆職之魏相焉。去壅蔽而力諫匈奴之伐，和陰陽而屢陳災異之狀，知大體之丙吉遇其配也。故稱之者曰：「丙魏有聲。」顧不偉與？有若裁處無滯之杜如晦焉。衆帷幄而剖決如流，官臺閣而規模創定，善謀之房玄齡資其斷也。故賢之者曰：「前有房杜。」顧不美與？守正不阿，嘗見推於宋璟；峭直不避，復見重於明皇；天下必肥，此韓休所以忠於唐也。忠義兼資，首建親征之策；忘身徇國，恥爲城下之盟；澶淵却狄，此寇準所以顯於宋也。之四公者，功在社稷，而澤潤生民，相業之表著，不有光於西土
translation_en:
…to become men of outstanding talent and sagely wisdom. The Guan–Shan region constituted ancient Yongzhou; its strategic terrain and natural advantages rank foremost under Heaven. Mount Hua and Mount Zhongnan hold its spiritual potency, while the Yellow River, Jing River, and Wei River spread its fine essence. Thus, those who emerged as sages and worthies, celebrated in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents, need no discussion here. Other men of manifold talents and accomplishments have appeared in profusion throughout successive dynasties; let us also leave them aside for now. Let us instead discuss examples from the Han and Tang onward, within the scope of your discerning question.
Those great ministers are the household stewards of the head of the ruling lineage, upon whom he relies to harmonize the primal forces and assist the transforming work of government. Among Yongzhou’s achievements in the chief councillorship were those of Wei Xiang, who oversaw all offices. He removed obstructions to the ruler’s access to information and vigorously remonstrated against a campaign against the Xiongnu; he harmonized yin and yang and repeatedly submitted accounts of calamities and anomalies. Bing Ji, who understood the larger concerns of government, found in him a worthy counterpart. Thus, those who praised them said, “Bing and Wei enjoyed renown.” Was this not great?
There was also Du Ruhui, who handled affairs without delay. In the command tent [?], he analyzed matters and reached decisions with flowing ease; serving in the central government, he established its institutional framework. Fang Xuanling, skilled in planning, relied upon his decisiveness. Thus, those who esteemed them said, “In former times there were Fang and Du.” Was this not admirable?
Upholding what was right without currying favor, Han Xiu won the commendation of Song Jing; unflinchingly forthright, he also earned the esteem of Emperor Minghuang. The realm would surely flourish: this was how Han Xiu served the Tang loyally. Endowed with both loyalty and righteousness, Kou Zhun was the first to propose that the emperor personally lead the campaign. Forgetting himself in devotion to the state, he considered a treaty made beneath the city walls a disgrace. He repelled the northern foe at Chanyuan: this was how Kou Zhun distinguished himself under the Song. These four gentlemen rendered meritorious service to the state, and their beneficence nourished the people. Did their conspicuous achievements as chief councillors not bring glory to the western lands…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
也乎將者三軍之司命所賴以攘夷安夏
者也雍之將略若廣屯田以困先零不煩
兵革而罣开之衆以降老成之趙充國可
尚也入虎穴以斬虜使餘威所及而鄯善
之子入質投筆之班超可嘉也郭子儀當
安史之亂大振軍威而收復兩京單騎見
虜亦所不辭非以身爲天下安危乎李晟
當奉天之變用師無犯而殄除反寇賊質
其家亦所不恤非棄家以再造社稷乎之
===
四公者威著華夷而勞定國家將略之卓
犖殆爲殊絶百代者也君子以通今博古
爲高窮經致用雍有其人矣天賦俊才而
三傳諸書並行於世設帳授徒而鄭盧諸
子皆出其門高才馬融其漢世之通儒也
詔撰詩書同異爲帝深嘉著書百萬餘言
傳父本業多聞之賈逵其漢世之儒宗也
杜預通明興廢而長曆一書所以行春秋
之義名之武庫可不謂之博耶張載精思
punctuated:
也乎？將者，三軍之司命，所賴以攘夷安夏者也。雍之將略，若廣屯田以困先零，不煩兵革而罣开之衆以降，老成之趙充國可尚也；入虎穴以斬虜使，餘威所及而鄯善之子入質，投筆之班超可嘉也。郭子儀當安史之亂，大振軍威而收復兩京，單騎見虜亦所不辭，非以身爲天下安危乎？李晟當奉天之變，用師無犯而殄除反寇，賊質其家亦所不恤，非棄家以再造社稷乎？之四公者，威著華夷而勞定國家，將略之卓犖，殆爲殊絶百代者也。
君子以通今博古爲高，窮經致用，雍有其人矣。天賦俊才，而三傳諸書並行於世；設帳授徒，而鄭盧諸子皆出其門。高才馬融，其漢世之通儒也。詔撰詩書同異，爲帝深嘉；著書百萬餘言，傳父本業。多聞之賈逵，其漢世之儒宗也。杜預通明興廢，而《長曆》一書所以行《春秋》之義，名之武庫，可不謂之博耶？張載精思
translation_en:
…did they not also bring glory to the western lands? A general holds the lives of the Three Armies in his hands; he is the one relied upon to repel the outsiders and secure the Chinese realm. Among Yong’s masters of military strategy, the seasoned Zhao Chongguo merits esteem: he expanded military farming settlements to wear down the Xianling, and the forces of Gua and Kai [?] surrendered without recourse to arms. Ban Chao, who cast aside his writing brush, merits praise: he entered the tiger’s den to behead the enemy’s envoys, and the lingering force of his威 prompted the ruler of Shanshan to send his son as a hostage. During the An–Shi Rebellion, Guo Ziyi greatly strengthened military power and recovered the two capitals. He did not shrink even from riding alone to meet the enemy. Did he not make his own person the pivot of the realm’s safety or peril? During the crisis at Fengtian, Li Sheng employed troops without allowing them to molest the people and exterminated the rebels. Even when the rebels took his family hostage, he gave it no heed. Did he not forsake his family to restore the state? These four gentlemen made their might known among Chinese and foreign peoples alike and labored to bring stability to the state. Their outstanding military strategy was perhaps unequaled through a hundred generations.
The gentleman esteems understanding the present and possessing broad knowledge of antiquity. In mastering the Classics and putting learning into practice, Yong had men equal to the task. Endowed by Heaven with exceptional talent, Ma Rong produced works on the Three Commentaries and other texts that circulated throughout the world; when he established his teaching seat and instructed disciples, such men as Zheng and Lu all studied under him. The gifted Ma Rong was surely a comprehensively learned Confucian scholar of the Han age. Commissioned by imperial decree to compile the similarities and differences in interpretations of the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents, Jia Kui received the emperor’s high praise. He wrote more than a million words, carrying on his father’s scholarly vocation. The widely learned Jia Kui was surely a leading Confucian authority of the Han age. Du Yu thoroughly understood the rise and fall of institutions, and his work, the Long Calendar (Changli), gave effect to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals. He was called an “arsenal”—could his learning fail to be described as broad? Zhang Zai pondered deeply…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
力踐而西銘一篇所以明仁孝之理律之
聖學可不謂之純耶數君子者儒術可稱
蓋亦關西之鄒魯矣君子以砥礪名節爲
尚隱居求志雍有其人矣鄭子眞躬耕谷
口而王鳳之聘不屈激貪厲懦可謂近古
之逸民梁鴻牧豕上林而長者之稱見異
琴詩自娛足稱儒者之高蹈泉石膏肓田
游巖之自道也高宗幸其門而比之四皓
不亦淸乎雲溪退士种放之自述也太宗
===
嘉其節而賜之存問不亦高乎數君子者
節介並著蓋亦後世之巢許矣夫即其建
立卓然固皆三秦之傑而要其成就所歸
豈無一定之論蓋出而用世者期於建功
而心術之微不可不察矣處而求志者期
於明道而禮義之中不可不究矣要之大
節可稱固不宜吹舉其細而責備賢者則
亦不可盡委之無言也封事可白矣而必
因許伯此何爲者雖言欲其行恐非聖人
punctuated:
力踐，而《西銘》一篇所以明仁孝之理，律之聖學，可不謂之純耶？數君子者，儒術可稱，蓋亦關西之鄒魯矣。
君子以砥礪名節爲尚，隱居求志，雍有其人矣。鄭子眞躬耕谷口，而王鳳之聘不屈，激貪厲懦，可謂近古之逸民。梁鴻牧豕上林，而長者之稱見異，琴詩自娛，足稱儒者之高蹈。泉石膏肓，田游巖之自道也；高宗幸其門，而比之四皓，不亦淸乎？雲溪退士，种放之自述也；太宗嘉其節，而賜之存問，不亦高乎？數君子者，節介並著，蓋亦後世之巢許矣。
夫即其建立卓然，固皆三秦之傑；而要其成就所歸，豈無一定之論？蓋出而用世者期於建功，而心術之微不可不察矣；處而求志者期於明道，而禮義之中不可不究矣。要之，大節可稱，固不宜吹舉其細；而責備賢者，則亦不可盡委之無言也。封事可白矣，而必因許伯，此何爲者？雖言欲其行，恐非聖人
translation_en:
…and put his learning earnestly into practice. His essay, the Western Inscription, illuminates the principles of benevolence and filial piety. Measured against the learning of the sages, could it not be called pure? These gentlemen deserve praise for their Confucian learning: they made the region west of the passes another Zou and Lu, the homelands of Mencius and Confucius.
The gentleman prizes the cultivation of reputation and integrity. Yong, too, has had men who lived in seclusion to pursue their aspirations. Zheng Zizhen personally tilled the fields at Gukou and would not yield to Wang Feng’s invitation to serve. Stirring the greedy to reform and the timid to resolve, he may be called a recluse approaching those of antiquity. Liang Hong tended pigs at Shanglin and was singled out for praise as a man of virtue. Finding pleasure in the zither and poetry, he fully deserves recognition as a lofty-minded Confucian recluse. An incurable passion for springs and rocks was Tian Youyan’s description of himself. Emperor Gaozong visited his door and compared him to the Four Hoary Elders: was he not pure? The Retired Scholar of Yunxi was Zhong Fang’s designation for himself. Emperor Taizong commended his integrity and graciously sent inquiries after his well-being: was he not lofty? These gentlemen were all renowned for their steadfast integrity; they were indeed the Chao Fu and Xu You of later ages.
Considering their outstanding accomplishments, all were unquestionably eminent men of the Three Qin region. Yet, when we assess the ultimate character of their achievements, can there be no settled judgment? Those who enter public service aim to establish meritorious achievements, but the subtleties of their motives must be examined. Those who remain in retirement to pursue their aspirations aim to illuminate the Way, but what accords with ritual propriety and righteousness must be investigated. In essence, when their integrity in major matters deserves praise, one certainly ought not to pick at their minor faults [?]. Yet, in holding worthy men to the standard of perfection, neither can one simply pass everything over in silence. A sealed memorial could have been submitted to the throne; why, then, insist on going through Xu Bo? Although the stated intention was to have its proposals put into effect, I fear this did not accord with the sage’s …

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
不比匪人之義也茲於弱翁不能無不滿
焉善乎韓休不干榮利守正不阿中外倚
其賢天下允其望卒之玄宗委任而社稷
是託其殆近古之遺直乎外夷可討矣而
要功於塞外亦可已者雖遠欲其服恐非
光武閉關謝西域之訓也茲於仲升不能
無過求焉善乎郭子儀忠誠體國至公無
我功蓋天下而上不疑權傾天下而朝不
忌卒之三朝倚重而完節令名其殆當時
===
之大人乎子厚之爲儒猶夫傳經也然逃
佛老而學有本原撤皐比而一變至道君
子謂廣居之示得孔門傳心之要也馬融
亦曰傳經矣設帳授徒而後列女樂何其
放乎奏頌之義果五經之旨與雖謂之五
經掃地可也子眞之隱居意避王氏也名
震京師而隱不逃世清激貪鄙而貞不絕
俗君子謂岩石之耕亦聖人可止之訓也
田游巖亦曰隱居矣聞召辭疾而深入箕
punctuated: 不比匪人之義也。茲於弱翁，不能無不滿焉。善乎韓休，不干榮利，守正不阿，中外倚其賢，天下允其望。卒之玄宗委任，而社稷是託，其殆近古之遺直乎！外夷可討矣，而要功於塞外，亦可已者。雖遠欲其服，恐非光武閉關謝西域之訓也。茲於仲升，不能無過求焉。善乎郭子儀，忠誠體國，至公無我，功蓋天下而上不疑，權傾天下而朝不忌。卒之三朝倚重，而完節令名，其殆當時之大人乎！子厚之爲儒，猶夫傳經也。然逃佛老而學有本原，撤皐比而一變至道。君子謂廣居之示，得孔門傳心之要也。馬融亦曰傳經矣，設帳授徒，而後列女樂，何其放乎！奏頌之義，果五經之旨與？雖謂之五經掃地可也。子眞之隱居，意避王氏也。名震京師而隱不逃世，清激貪鄙而貞不絕俗。君子謂岩石之耕，亦聖人可止之訓也。田游巖亦曰隱居矣，聞召辭疾而深入箕
translation_en:
…the principle of not associating with unworthy men. In this respect, one cannot help feeling dissatisfied with Ruoweng. Admirable indeed was Han Xiu! He sought neither glory nor profit, upheld what was right, and refused to flatter. Those at court and outside it relied upon his worth, and all under Heaven acknowledged his reputation. In the end, Xuanzong entrusted him with office and committed the altars of soil and grain to his care. Was he perhaps an heir to the uprightness of antiquity?

Foreign peoples might indeed be chastised, but seeking military merit beyond the frontier was something that could have been forgone. Although the aim was to secure the submission of distant peoples, this was perhaps inconsistent with Guangwu’s example of closing the passes and declining involvement with the Western Regions. In this respect, one cannot refrain from holding Zhongsheng to a stricter standard. Admirable indeed was Guo Ziyi! Loyal and sincere, he devoted himself to the state, utterly impartial and without selfishness. His achievements surpassed all others under Heaven, yet his sovereign did not distrust him; his power overshadowed all others, yet the court did not resent him. In the end, three successive reigns relied heavily upon him, and he preserved his integrity and good name. Was he perhaps a great man of his age?

Zihou’s practice as a Confucian likewise involved transmitting the classics. Yet he escaped Buddhism and Daoism, giving his learning a firm foundation; he removed the tiger-skin seat of a lecturer and, with a single transformation, attained the Way. The gentleman holds that his teaching concerning the ‘spacious dwelling’ grasped the essentials of the transmission of the mind in the school of Confucius. Ma Rong, too, was said to transmit the classics. He set up a teaching curtain and instructed disciples, yet arrayed female musicians behind him. How unrestrained he was! Did the purport of the eulogy he submitted truly accord with the intent of the Five Classics? One might even say that he dragged the Five Classics into the dust.

Zizhen’s intention in living in seclusion was to avoid the Wang clan. His name resounded through the capital, yet in retirement he did not flee the world; his purity stirred the greedy and base to reform, yet his rectitude did not sever him from ordinary society. The gentleman holds that his farming among the rocks likewise exemplified the sage’s teaching to withdraw when withdrawal was appropriate. Tian Youyan, too, was said to live in seclusion. On hearing a summons, he pleaded illness and withdrew deep into Mount Ji…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
山何其固乎膏肓之對非聖人之中也雖
謂之鳥獸同羣可也雖然此就數子言之
也論治者必稽諸古考德者宜法乎上韓
休遺直矣而制禮作樂尚有岐周之元聖
子儀大人矣而相湯伐夏尚有莘野之天
民壤駟赤秦州之產也游孔門而長於詩
書方諸子厚其見而知之者乎夷齊輩昌
之隱也登西山而采薇以食較諸子眞其
百世之師矣乎於乎心術之微難知久矣
===
禮義之中難言久矣據其陳跡而方諸大
道雖不能無指於其中而皎皎白璧掩其
微瑕則固珪璋瑚璉之器也是故如晦諸
君子所不槩論也子厚曰求爲賢人而不
求爲聖人秦漢以來學者大病然則定尚
友之極可不於三代之前哉謏聞劣識奚
足方人敬以復明問焉爾
第五問
姜葢
punctuated:
山，何其固乎！膏肓之對，非聖人之中也，雖謂之鳥獸同羣可也。雖然，此就數子言之也。論治者必稽諸古，考德者宜法乎上。韓休遺直矣，而制禮作樂，尚有岐周之元聖；子儀大人矣，而相湯伐夏，尚有莘野之天民。壤駟赤，秦州之產也，游孔門而長於詩書，方諸子厚，其見而知之者乎？夷齊，輩昌之隱也，登西山而采薇以食，較諸子眞，其百世之師矣乎？於乎！心術之微難知久矣，禮義之中難言久矣。據其陳跡而方諸大道，雖不能無指於其中，而皎皎白璧掩其微瑕，則固珪璋瑚璉之器也。是故如晦諸君子所不槩論也。子厚曰：「求爲賢人而不求爲聖人，秦漢以來學者大病。」然則定尚友之極，可不於三代之前哉？謏聞劣識，奚足方人？敬以復明問焉爾。

第五問
姜葢
translation_en:
…Mountain—how obstinate he was! His reply about an incurable passion for reclusion did not accord with the sage’s mean. One might even describe him as keeping company with birds and beasts. Yet these remarks concern only the several men just discussed. Those who discuss government must consult antiquity; those who assess virtue should take the highest as their standard. Han Xiu preserved the uprightness of antiquity, yet for instituting rites and composing music there was the great sage of Zhou at Qi. Ziyi was a great man, yet for assisting Tang in attacking Xia there was the Heaven-endowed man of the fields of Shen. Rangsi Chi was a native of Qinzhou; he studied in Confucius’s school and excelled in the Odes and Documents. Compared with Zihou, was he not one who knew the Way through seeing the sage himself? Boyi and Shuqi were recluses of Beichang [?]; they climbed the Western Mountain and gathered wild vetch to eat. Compared with Zizhen, were they not teachers for a hundred generations?

Alas! The subtleties of the heart’s workings have long been difficult to discern, and the proper mean of ritual and righteousness has long been difficult to articulate. If we take the surviving traces of their deeds and compare them with the Great Way, we cannot avoid finding faults among them. Yet their gleaming white jade eclipses its slight blemishes: they are assuredly men of the caliber of ritual jade tablets and sacrificial vessels. Thus Ruhui and the other gentlemen cannot be judged indiscriminately. Zihou said: “To seek to become a worthy but not to seek to become a sage has been the great failing of scholars since the Qin and Han.” Then, in establishing the highest standard for befriending the ancients, must we not look to the time before the Three Dynasties? With my scant learning and inferior understanding, how could I be qualified to assess others? I respectfully offer this in response to your discerning question.

Fifth Policy Question
Jiang Gai

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭王　批〔區畫精詳皆切實用可以爲矣〕
考試官教諭盧　批〔革弊興利井然有條足識時務者〕
考試官學正丘　批〔可行之言錄之〕
天下之事有其法無其人弊不可與革也
有其名無其實利不可與興也夫弊不革
者非法不立也不得其人則法弛而弊斯
生矣利不興者非名不存也不核其實則
名虛而利斯匱矣是故脩廢法者在得人
緣虛名者在核實得人則勵精之政施而
弊自革矣核實則脩復之務舉而利自興
===
矣執事以足食足兵之策下詢承學是欲
聞經國之遠猷籌邊之至計也草茅之士
何足以知之然言及之而不言可乎請悉
心以對夫禦戎之道二戰守而已矣預備
之道二兵食而已矣古人慮餽餉不足以
供軍士也於是有屯田之政焉無事則散
之而爲農有事則合之而爲兵內以紓轉
輸之苦外以足邊餉之需足食之道未有
punctuated:
同考試官教諭王　批〔區畫精詳，皆切實用，可以爲矣。〕
考試官教諭盧　批〔革弊興利，井然有條，足識時務者。〕
考試官學正丘　批〔可行之言，錄之。〕
天下之事，有其法無其人，弊不可與革也；有其名無其實，利不可與興也。夫弊不革者，非法不立也；不得其人，則法弛而弊斯生矣。利不興者，非名不存也；不核其實，則名虛而利斯匱矣。是故脩廢法者在得人，緣虛名者在核實。得人則勵精之政施，而弊自革矣；核實則脩復之務舉，而利自興矣。執事以足食足兵之策下詢承學，是欲聞經國之遠猷、籌邊之至計也。草茅之士，何足以知之？然言及之而不言，可乎？請悉心以對。夫禦戎之道二：戰、守而已矣。預備之道二：兵、食而已矣。古人慮餽餉不足以供軍士也，於是有屯田之政焉。無事則散之而爲農，有事則合之而爲兵，內以紓轉輸之苦，外以足邊餉之需。足食之道，未有
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: 〔The planning is precise and thorough, and all of it meets practical needs. It can be put into effect.〕
Examiner Lu, Instructor, comments: 〔Eliminating abuses and promoting benefits are treated in an orderly, systematic fashion: the work of someone well acquainted with current affairs.〕
Examiner Qiu, School Instructor, comments: 〔These proposals are practicable. Record them.〕
In the affairs of the realm, if there are regulations but no suitable men, abuses cannot be eliminated; if there are names but no substance, benefits cannot be promoted. Failure to eliminate abuses does not arise from a failure to establish regulations. Without suitable men, regulations fall into disuse, and abuses consequently arise. Failure to promote benefits does not arise from a lack of nominal provision. Unless actual conditions are examined, names are empty, and benefits consequently fall short. Thus, restoring neglected regulations depends on finding suitable men; where empty names are relied upon [?], actual conditions must be examined. With suitable men, vigorous government is implemented, and abuses are naturally eliminated. When actual conditions are examined, the work of restoration proceeds, and benefits naturally arise.
You, honored examiners, have condescended to question us students about policies for ensuring sufficient food and troops, wishing to hear far-reaching plans for governing the state and the best strategies for managing the frontier. How could a man of humble station know enough about these matters? Yet, when invited to speak of them, could I remain silent? Allow me to reply with all my heart.
There are only two ways of resisting hostile peoples: fighting and defending. There are only two essentials of preparedness: troops and food. The ancients feared that supplies would be insufficient to support their soldiers, and therefore instituted military agricultural colonies. When there was no emergency, the men dispersed to farm; when an emergency arose, they assembled as soldiers. Within the country, this eased the burdens of transporting supplies; on the frontier, it met the need for military provisions. Among methods of ensuring sufficient food, there has never been …

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
踰於此者文帝海內致富庶矣募丁民以
耕塞下君子每以務本而稱其賢武帝募
南無王庭矣遣戰士以屯燉煌君子不以
黷武而略其善趙充國屯兵金城用以破
先零也卒收坐困之功諸葛亮雜耕渭濵
用以圖中原也遂致羸餘之積朱子謂屯
田實邊最寛民力者誠爲不易之論也屯
政不有可稽者乎古人恐乘騎不足以給
行伍也於是有牧馬之政焉司牧必專其
===
職孳息以致其富上以壯萬乘之威下以
給三軍之用足兵之道莫有過於此者漢
制內地則勸民養馬以復卒邊地則縱民
畜牧而不禁此則牧之於民而用之於官
唐制官出其直令兵以自買及不任戰許
賣以吏市此則牧之於官而用之於民宋
制英宗以前始置諸監給地牧馬而牧之
於官神宗以後諸監既廢仰給市馬而牧
之於民若周制八軍之馬牧之民公家之
punctuated: 踰於此者。文帝海內致富庶矣，募丁民以耕塞下，君子每以務本而稱其賢。武帝募南無王庭矣，遣戰士以屯燉煌，君子不以黷武而略其善。趙充國屯兵金城，用以破先零也，卒收坐困之功；諸葛亮雜耕渭濵，用以圖中原也，遂致羸餘之積。朱子謂屯田實邊最寛民力者，誠爲不易之論也。屯政不有可稽者乎？古人恐乘騎不足以給行伍也，於是有牧馬之政焉。司牧必專其職，孳息以致其富，上以壯萬乘之威，下以給三軍之用。足兵之道，莫有過於此者。漢制，內地則勸民養馬以復卒，邊地則縱民畜牧而不禁，此則牧之於民而用之於官。唐制，官出其直，令兵以自買，及不任戰，許賣以吏市，此則牧之於官而用之於民。宋制，英宗以前，始置諸監，給地牧馬，而牧之於官；神宗以後，諸監既廢，仰給市馬，而牧之於民。若周制，八軍之馬牧之民，公家之
translation_en:
…surpasses this. Under Emperor Wen, the realm had attained wealth and abundance, yet he recruited able-bodied commoners to cultivate land beneath the frontier fortifications. Men of discernment have always praised his worth for attending to the foundation of livelihood. Under Emperor Wu, no royal court remained south of the desert [?], yet he dispatched soldiers to establish agricultural colonies at Dunhuang. Men of discernment do not let his excessive warfare obscure this merit. Zhao Chongguo stationed troops to farm at Jincheng in order to defeat the Xianling, and ultimately succeeded in wearing them down without fighting. Zhuge Liang had his troops cultivate alongside the inhabitants on the banks of the Wei River in order to recover the Central Plain, and thereby accumulated surplus provisions. Master Zhu said that establishing agricultural colonies to strengthen the frontier afforded the greatest relief to the people's labor. This is indeed an incontrovertible judgment. Are there not precedents in the administration of agricultural colonies that can be consulted?

The ancients feared that there would not be enough mounts to supply the ranks, and therefore instituted policies for raising horses. Those responsible for pasturage were required to devote themselves to their duties, increasing the herds through breeding. Above, this strengthened the might of the sovereign of ten thousand chariots; below, it supplied the needs of the armies. No method of providing adequately for the troops surpasses this. Under the Han system, people in the interior were encouraged to raise horses in return for exemption from military service, while those in the borderlands were permitted to raise livestock without restriction. Thus horses were raised by the people and used by the government. Under the Tang system, the government supplied the purchase price and ordered soldiers to buy horses themselves. When the horses became unfit for battle, their sale was permitted, with officials handling the market transactions [?]. Thus horses were raised under government auspices and used by the people. Under the Song system, before Emperor Yingzong, the various horse directorates were first established and allotted land for pasturing horses, so that horses were raised by the government. After Emperor Shenzong, once the directorates had been abolished, supplies depended on purchasing horses, so that horses were raised by the people. As for the Zhou system, the horses of the eight armies were pastured by the people, while those belonging to the ruling house…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
馬養之校人者始爲不易之法耳馬政不
有可考者乎仰惟我
國家稽古定制建衛置兵屯田專監司之職
馬政設寺苑之官立法可謂詳且密矣但
時易而人玩法久而弊生屯田馬政固有
不能如前日者矣貧者鬻於富室以救目
前之急弱者侵於豪右以失身後之產占
役於私門以奪其力侵漁於科剋以盡其
有甚至那移出納藉名支領屯田之政廢
===
矣欲食之足得乎牧地淪於兼幷埋没而
不清牧夫苦於征求逃亡而未復損折者
失於清查孳息者事乎虛報甚至狡猾巧
蔽豪强怙恃馬政之弊滋矣欲兵之足得
乎意當此因循之後而安於故常之習者
何以爲禦戎之計哉要之在重屯田馬政
之職使之得以展布而不撓其法則脩舉
之政興而廢弛之患祛核實之政舉而虛
文之弊革琴瑟更調而大化可張矣誠於
punctuated: 馬養之校人者，始爲不易之法耳。馬政不有可考者乎？仰惟我國家稽古定制，建衛置兵，屯田專監司之職，馬政設寺苑之官，立法可謂詳且密矣。但時易而人玩，法久而弊生，屯田馬政固有不能如前日者矣。貧者鬻於富室，以救目前之急；弱者侵於豪右，以失身後之產；占役於私門，以奪其力；侵漁於科剋，以盡其有。甚至那移出納，藉名支領，屯田之政廢矣，欲食之足，得乎？牧地淪於兼幷，埋没而不清；牧夫苦於征求，逃亡而未復；損折者失於清查，孳息者事乎虛報。甚至狡猾巧蔽，豪强怙恃，馬政之弊滋矣，欲兵之足，得乎？意當此因循之後，而安於故常之習者，何以爲禦戎之計哉？要之，在重屯田馬政之職，使之得以展布而不撓其法，則脩舉之政興，而廢弛之患祛；核實之政舉，而虛文之弊革。琴瑟更調，而大化可張矣。誠於
translation_en:
…horses maintained by the Director of Studs (xiaoren): only this constitutes an enduring system. Are there not precedents in horse administration that can be examined?

I humbly reflect that our dynasty consulted antiquity in establishing its institutions, creating guards and stationing troops. It assigned particular responsibility for military agricultural colonies to the surveillance officials and established court and pasturage officials for horse administration. Its regulations may indeed be called detailed and comprehensive. Yet as times change, people grow negligent; as regulations age, abuses arise. The administration of military agricultural colonies and horses has consequently fallen short of its former condition. The poor sell their land to wealthy households to relieve their immediate distress; the weak suffer encroachment by powerful families and lose the property they would leave to their descendants. Men are appropriated for service in private households, depriving the colonies of their labor; extortion through levies and deductions exhausts their possessions. Funds and supplies are even diverted in the handling of receipts and disbursements, and drawn under borrowed names. The administration of military agricultural colonies has fallen into ruin. Can sufficient provisions then be secured?

Pasturelands fall into the hands of engrossing landholders, their status obscured and never clarified. Herdsmen, oppressed by demands and exactions, flee and have not returned. Losses of horses escape proper investigation, while increases through breeding become the subject of false reports. Cunning men even contrive concealments, and the powerful rely on their influence. Abuses in horse administration multiply. Can adequate military resources then be secured?

I consider that, after such prolonged neglect, those who remain content with habitual practices can hardly devise plans for defending against hostile peoples. The essential point is to give greater weight to the offices responsible for military agricultural colonies and horse administration, allowing their officials to exercise their abilities without obstructing their measures. Then measures for restoring proper administration will flourish, and the harm caused by neglect will be removed; verification of actual conditions will be undertaken, and the abuse of empty paperwork eliminated. Once the zithers are retuned, great transformation can unfold. If, indeed, with regard to…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
司屯田者假之以便宜之權如充國之在
漢孔明之在蜀久任以行其法私鬻者必
復侵占者必治私役者必革侵漁者必禁
而又稽其出入禁其冒破如此則權重而
令行令行而弊革行之數年其效必有可
觀者雖紅腐之富不可以驟致而邊餉亦
不至告匱矣尚何屯政之不可行哉司寺
苑者假之以便宜之權如非子之在秦萬
歲之在唐專職以行其志埋没者必清逃
===
亡者必復虛報者必究損折者必查□□
點閱有法牝字以時如此則政專而法□
法立而利興遲之歲月其政必有可□□
雖雲錦之盛難以遽得而騎操亦不致告
乏矣又何馬政之不可脩哉夫屯田不足
以盡食馬政不足以盡兵而執事□□以二
者爲問者無乃舉其重以例其餘□□□
此則足食足兵之計猶有可言者矣□□
鹽之法廣水田之利去冗食之費□□□
punctuated: 司屯田者假之以便宜之權，如充國之在漢、孔明之在蜀，久任以行其法。私鬻者必復，侵占者必治，私役者必革，侵漁者必禁，而又稽其出入，禁其冒破。如此則權重而令行，令行而弊革。行之數年，其效必有可觀者。雖紅腐之富不可以驟致，而邊餉亦不至告匱矣，尚何屯政之不可行哉？司寺苑者假之以便宜之權，如非子之在秦、萬歲之在唐，專職以行其志。埋没者必清，逃亡者必復，虛報者必究，損折者必查。□□點閱有法，牝字以時。如此則政專而法□，法立而利興。遲之歲月，其政必有可□□。雖雲錦之盛難以遽得，而騎操亦不致告乏矣，又何馬政之不可脩哉？夫屯田不足以盡食，馬政不足以盡兵，而執事□□以二者爲問者，無乃舉其重以例其餘□□□？此則足食足兵之計猶有可言者矣。□□鹽之法，廣水田之利，去冗食之費□□□
translation_en:
…grant those administering military agricultural colonies discretionary authority, as Chongguo had under the Han and Kongming in Shu, and retain them in office long enough to carry out their policies. Land privately sold must be recovered; encroachment must be punished; the private exploitation of labor must be abolished; and extortion must be prohibited. Furthermore, audit receipts and expenditures and prohibit fraudulent disbursements. Thus, with substantial authority, orders will be enforced; with orders enforced, abuses will be eliminated. After several years, the results will surely be appreciable. Although abundance so great that grain reddens and rots cannot be achieved at once, provisions for the frontier will at least not run short. What, then, could prevent the administration of agricultural colonies from being put into effect?
Grant those administering the Court of the Imperial Stud and its pastures discretionary authority, as Feizi had in Qin and Wansui under the Tang, and give them undivided responsibility to carry out their intentions. Concealed holdings must be brought to light; fugitives must be brought back; false reports must be investigated; and losses must be examined. [Illegible] inspections must follow established procedures, and mares must be bred at the proper season [?]. Thus administrative responsibility will be concentrated and regulations [illegible]; once regulations are established, benefits will follow. Given time, this administration will surely have something worthy of [illegible]. Although herds as splendid as cloud-patterned brocade cannot quickly be obtained, cavalry training will at least not suffer a shortage of horses. What, then, could prevent horse administration from being set in order?
Military agricultural colonies do not encompass every aspect of provisioning, nor does horse administration encompass every aspect of military affairs. Yet you, honored examiners, [illegible] have asked about these two matters: is this not to take the most important as examples for the rest [illegible]? There is therefore still more to say about plans for securing sufficient food and troops. [Illegible] the salt regulations, expand the benefits of irrigated fields, and eliminate the expense of feeding superfluous dependents [illegible]…

title: 嘉靖二十八年陝西鄉試錄
text:
衆而用之者舒則倉廪無不充矣繕器械
之利勸簡閱之法明賞罰之格養之者厚
